questions.stem: If \(f(x) = x^2-9x+14\), then the asymptotes of the curve with equation \(y=\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\) are:
questions.hint: Vertical asymptotes occur where \(f(x)=0\) (the denominator vanishes); the horizontal asymptote is found from the behaviour of \(\frac1{f(x)}\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\).

steps.explain: Factorise \(f(x)\) to find where it equals zero — these give the vertical asymptotes of \(y=1/f(x)\).
As \(x\to\pm\infty\), \(f(x)\to\infty\), so \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\to 0\) — this gives the horizontal asymptote.

questions.stem: Which of the following equations does NOT result in a graph that is a function?
questions.hint: Use the vertical-line test: a function gives only one y-value for each allowed x-value.

steps.explain: The first three equations assign one y-value to each allowed x. For the circle, solve for y.
For most x-values between −5 and 5, the circle has both a positive and a negative y-value.
steps.work: For example, x = 0 gives y = 5 or y = −5

steps.explain: A vertical line through x = 0 meets the circle twice, so it fails the vertical-line test.
steps.work: The circle relation is not a function of x.

keyPoints.text: NOT result in a graph that is a function
keyPoints.note: Check whether one x-value can give two different y-values.

questions.stem: What values can \(x\) possibly take in the formula \(y=\sqrt{6-3x}\)?

meta.source: Sydney Girls High School Year 10 Yearly Examination 2011

questions.hint: For a real square root, the expression underneath must be at least zero. Solve that inequality and remember to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative.

keyPoints.note: Require the radicand (6-3x) to be non-negative.

steps.explain: For y to be a real number, the radicand cannot be negative.
Subtract 6 from both sides, then divide by \(-3\). Dividing by a negative reverses the inequality.
At x=2 the radicand is zero, so the endpoint is included. Smaller values make it positive.
